title: Day 79 · Week 11, Day 2 — Physiology: her skin — the dark line, the mask and the sunscreen trial, what altitude and snow add, six trials of stretch-mark creams, and the itch without a rash that changes the birth plan
summary: Why pregnancy changes the skin: placental oestrogen, progesterone and melanocyte-stimulating signals, a larger blood volume, and rapid stretch. Pigment changes are near-universal (93% in a 2026 cross-sectional study): linea nigra, darker areolae, darkening moles (a markedly changing mole still needs checking) and melasma, which needs ultraviolet light — in one Moroccan study daily SPF 50+ broad-spectrum sunscreen cut new cases to 2.7% against a historical 53% (Lakhdar 2007, historical control). WHO: UV rises ~10% per 1,000 m and fresh snow reflects up to 80%. Palmar erythema and spider angiomas are oestrogen effects. Stretch marks affected 52% of 309 first-time mothers, more often younger women and those with higher BMI, more weight gain or a heavier baby (Atwal 2006); across six trials and 800 women no topical preparation clearly prevented them (Cochrane, RR 0.74, 0.53–1.03). Postpartum shedding at 2–4 months is normal. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — itch on palms and soles, no rash, worse at night — affects ~0.7% in the UK; stillbirth risk tracks peak bile acids: 0.13% below 40 µmol/L, 0.28% at 40–99, 3.44% at ≥100 (Ovadia 2019, IPD 5,269 women), which sets the timing of birth; ursodeoxycholic acid did not reduce adverse outcomes (PITCHES, 605 women).
action: Add under the red flags in the pregnancy file: "Itching on palms or soles, no rash, worse at night: call the practice that week and ask for bile acids and liver function tests." Put a broad-spectrum SPF 50 sunscreen in the travel bag and a second by the front door.
